THE WORLD AND THE PATH: ABHINAVA'S ONTOLOGY AND SOTERIOLOGY

The Śivatattva, the kañcukas, the jīvanmukta, and the closing sum — the completion of the recognition-thesis (V3J–P)

  • 026-08-11. The recognition-thesis is an epistemology (knowledge is the felt self-awareness) and a
  • taphysics (action and causation are the self-awareness's agency). But it is also an ontology (what
  • e world is) and a soteriology (how one is liberated). These are the final regions Abhinava adds, in
  • e āgamādhikāra (V3J–M) and the tattvasaṅgrahādhikāra (V3N–P). This essay expounds them, and shows how
  • ey complete the recognition-thesis: the world is the self-articulation of consciousness, and the
  • beration is its recognition.*

1. Why the ontology comes last: the role of the āgama

  • e IPVV's own order is precise, and it is the key to the āgamādhikāra:
  • jñānādhikāra — establish the self, the powers, the knower, by argument.
  • kriyādhikāra — establish action, the will, causality, by argument.
  • āgamādhikāra — now the categories (the tattvas) are given by the teaching, because reason
  • nnot reach the whole.
"Our perception is not an omniscient eye; our inference lacks the pervasion that would reach every
thing. Neither can grasp the whole. Only the āgama — the revealed teaching — can do so; for it is
nothing other than the re-recollection of the un-contracted manifestation of the supreme Lord." (V3J)
  • The method.** Reason and revelation are not rivals in the IPVV; they are sequential. Reason
  • tablishes the self (the first two adhikāras); the teaching supplies the world (the categories),
  • cause the whole world cannot be reached by reason alone. The āgamādhikāra comes last because it
  • mpletes what reason began — it fills in the content reason cannot reach. This is the IPVV's own
  • ternal epistemology of its own method.

2. The Śivatattva as the body of every category (V3J)

  • e pivot of the āgamādhikāra:
"At the heart of it all is the Śivatattva, which is the body of every category... knowledge and
action — manifestation and reflexive-awareness — are un-joined, inseparable; and this inseparable
pair is the supreme form of all beings." (V3J)
  • The claim.* The Śivatattva is not one category among others; it is the *body of every category. The
  • ole world — from Śiva down to the earth — is woven into the one reality (the "warp and woof,"
  • aprota). And its essence is the inseparable pair: knowledge (manifestation) + action (reflexive-
  • areness) — the jñāna-kriyā pair that the argument-sections already established.
  • The systematic point.** The categories are not a separate cosmology. They are the unfolding of the
  • e reality whose essence the argument-sections found in the self. The āgama fills in the world as
  • e self-articulation of what the arguments found in the self. The Śivatattva is where the
  • cognition-thesis becomes an ontology: the world is the Lord's own body.
  • The objection, answered.** "How can Śiva, who is beyond māyā, appear as the primary category in the
  • rld of mind?" The answer: self-shining is freedom, and the downward-pervasion of that self-shining is
  • eation itself. The self-shining Śiva, in his freedom, pours himself downward into the world — and
  • at pouring is the world. There is nothing arbitrary; it is the very nature of the light to shine
  • rth.

3. The kañcukas and the malas (V3K/L)

  • scending from the pure realm, the IPVV comes to the bound knower, and to what hides the pure self.

3.1 The kañcukas (the coverings)

  • e pure self is covered by five limiting sheaths — the kañcukas, literally the "armours":
  • niyati (fixity): the binding of each effect to its own cause — the seed causes the sprout, not
  • e pot. In truth, "the Lord alone shines forth as 'this is the cause of that'; the binding is a
  • vering laid over the reality by the limited knower" (V3K).
  • kāla (time): the apparent sequence.
  • rāga (attachment): "the whole flux of the mind, rooted in desire and envy" (V3K).
  • vidyā (limited knowledge).
  • kalā (limited agency).
  • The systematic point.** The kañcukas are the finite architecture — the determinate contractions by
  • ich the one manifests as a bound knower. They are real (the world is not illusion) but they are the
  • verings of the pure self, not its essence.

3.2 The bound knower and the malas

  • e bound knower (the paśu, the "animal") is "blind by māyā, wandering in saṃsāra, bound by his
  • tions" (V3L). Over against him stands the pati (the Lord), "whose own-members — the beings of the
  • rld — are his own." The bound one is bound because he has suffered the loss of freedom of the
  • areness — he has become un-aware of his own freedom, caught in the objects.
  • e three stains (mala) that bind:
  • āṇava (finitude): the sense of the limited "I."
  • māyīya (objectivity): the manifestation of the distinct known as other than the self.
  • kārma (action): the binding by deeds.
  • The systematic point.** The bondage is not the mere finite architecture (the kañcukas are real); it
  • the misreading — the loss of freedom, the un-awareness of the self as the Lord. This is the
  • cognition-thesis's soteriological face: bondage is misrecognition.

4. The states of the bound knower (V3M)

  • e bound knower lives in a round of states — waking, dream, deep sleep — which are the texture of his
  • ndage:
  • The void (pralayākala): the dissolved knower, absorbed in the void, "with only the barest trace
  • an 'I'" (V3M).
  • Deep sleep (suṣupta): a resting in the mere void or the breath, "where consciousness is put to
  • eep by māyā" (V3M). Its many forms — sleep from fatigue, fainting, intoxication, even samādhi —
  • e all species of this one state.
  • The dream (svapna): "the mind's own making, a clear appearance that the waking refutes" (V3M).
  • The waking (jāgrat): the common creation, the firm external world shared by all the knowers.
  • The systematic point.** The states are the descent of the Lord through the forms of the world. The
  • und knower's descent is the Lord's descent — the same consciousness, contracted into the states.

5. The bond and the liberation (V3O)

  • e heart of the tattvasaṅgraha is the relation of the bound one to the Lord — and it turns on a single
  • ct:

5.1 The paśu's creation is un-common

  • e bound one does not merely suffer the world; he creates it, after his own fashion — but his
  • eation is un-common (asādhāraṇī), private, per-knower, per-moment, vanishing with him.
"The bound one's own power is hidden from him — he is other-dependent — and only the Lord-ness can
awaken it. The whole difference of bound and liberated hangs on a single fact: the bound one does
not know his own power. He forgets that the world he builds is built with the Lord's own
materials." (V3O)

5.2 The construction-action is the bond

  • y it the māyā-power binds the animal" (V3O). Even the seemingly free constructions — "I, the king,
  • and," "I have slain my enemy" — are, on inspection, other-dependent; the bound one's freedom is only
  • parent, resting on the Lord's.

5.3 The Lord's creation is common

  • ainst this stands the Lord's own creation — common (sādhāraṇā), clear-manifestation, never
  • nstructed, always whole. And there is a path out of the prison: the abandonment of construction.
"When, by the thinning of the constructions and the gathering of the mind to one point, the bound
one comes to the 'I-this' of the Lord, his animal-ness is destroyed and the Lord-ness shines." (V3O)

6. The closing sum: the jīvanmukta and the recognition-path (V3P)

  • e IPVV closes on the transmission and the path.

6.1 The transmission (the guru-paramparā)

  • e teaching comes from three sources — the self (svataḥ), the śāstra (śāstrataḥ), and the guru
  • urutaḥ). And Abhinava is stern about the guru:
"The book-studied knowledges, without the guru-order, practicing and teaching, ripen long in hell."
(V3P)
  • e line runs from the ādi-Śrīkaṇṭhanātha down through Durvāsa and Tryambakāditya, the mental sons who
  • rry the un-precedented, effort-less word.

6.2 The recognition-path

"Since liberation is from the recognition alone, all the elaborate effort-yogas are useless here;
this is the clear means, effort-less, un-undertaken, yet bearing the great fruit." (V3P)
  • e breath-controls are artificial; "the un-made reality does not yield to a sixteenth part of such
  • fort." The recognition cuts through all of it.

6.3 The jīvanmukta

  • e fruit is the while-living-liberated:
"The one who, even in the body, is already free, and who at the fall of the body is simply the
supreme Lord. This, Abhinavagupta says, is the most wondrous thing of all — liberation in this very
life." (V3P)

6.4 The closing image

"The lover stands near, sought by the slender woman; but as long as he is not recognized, he cannot
be enjoyed. So the world-Lord, always present, always near, is not experienced in his own splendor
until the recognition arises. The world has him before it, and yet does not see him, until the
single act of recognition turns the un-known nearness into the joy of union." (V3P)
  • e whole IPVV closes on the recognition — the turning of the near into the enjoyed, the felt
  • -cognition of the self. The soteriology completes the epistemology: the recognition that is the
  • sence of light is also the path to liberation, and its fruit is the jīvanmukta.

7. The map of the ontology and soteriology

  • Region | Locus | Content |
  • -------|-------|---------|
  • The role of the āgama | V3J | the teaching supplies the whole that reason cannot reach |
  • The Śivatattva | V3J | the body of every category; the jñāna-kriyā pair |
  • The kañcukas | V3K | niyati, kāla, rāga, vidyā, kalā — the coverings |
  • The malas | V3L | āṇava, māyīya, kārma — the stains; the paśu and the pati |
  • The states | V3M | the void, deep sleep, dream, waking — the descent |
  • The bond | V3O | the paśu's un-common creation; the construction-action |
  • The liberation | V3O/P | the abandonment of construction; the jīvanmukta |
  • The transmission | V3P | the guru-paramparā; the recognition-path |
  • The thesis.** The ontology and soteriology complete the recognition-thesis. The world is the
  • lf-articulation of consciousness (the Śivatattva as the body of every category); the bondage is the
  • sreading (the loss of freedom, the un-awareness of the self as the Lord); and the liberation is the
  • cognition — the turning of the near into the enjoyed, the felt re-cognition of the self. The IPVV
  • es not stop at the epistemology; it builds the world and the path, and closes on the jīvanmukta.
  • is is the completion of the system, and it is the soteriology that neither the IPK nor Ratié's book
  • velops.
  • his is the ontology-and-soteriology essay. The āgamādhikāra supplies the world (the Śivatattva as
  • e body of every category; the kañcukas; the malas; the states); the tattvasaṅgraha supplies the path
  • he abandonment of construction; the recognition; the jīvanmukta; the guru-paramparā). The whole
  • oses on the recognition — the turning of the near into the enjoyed. This is the completion of the
  • cognition-thesis, the soteriology that neither the IPK nor Ratié develops.*
